sources.title: Molecular Choreography of Acute Exercise
sources.population: 36 well-characterized adult volunteers; cohort includes insulin-resistant participants.
sources.design: Longitudinal acute exercise challenge with dense blood multi-omics and integrative analyses.
sources.sampling_times: Pre-exercise and 2, 15, 30, and 60 minutes in recovery.
sources.biomarkers: Plasma untargeted metabolomics (728 metabolites), semi-targeted lipidomics (710 complex lipids), plasma proteomics/immunome, and PBMC transcriptomics.
sources.key_finding: Time-series integration identified coordinated early energy-metabolism, oxidative-stress and immune-response signals, followed by later homeostasis and repair. Many exercise responses were dampened or reversed in insulin-resistant participants. The study also developed models for fitness-related measures using resting analytes.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No infection incidence or post-exercise immune functional endpoint. Resting biomarkers were used to predict peak VO2/fitness measures, not infection susceptibility.
sources.validation: Multi-omic time-course and internal association/prediction analyses; no external validation of an infection-risk model and no pathogen challenge.
sources.limitations: Small cohort and short recovery follow-up; systemic metabolite/lipid changes are not themselves evidence of immune suppression or altered pathogen defense. Pathway integration does not establish that circulating metabolites mediate PBMC function.
sources.evidence_anchor: Abstract; Results, ‘Multi-omic changes in response to exercise’ and PBMC gene-expression sections; Methods, cohort and sampling design.
sources.integrity_notes: Bibliographic record and DOI verified through PubMed/PMC and publisher indexing. Limited title-specific notice search found no matching correction/retraction, not an exhaustive audit.

sources.title: Vitamin D status modulates innate immune responses and metabolomic profiles following acute prolonged cycling
sources.authors: Arwel W. Jones, Adrian Mironas, Luis A. J. Mur, Manfred Beckmann, Rhys Thatcher, Glen Davison
sources.population: 23 healthy recreationally active men, age 25 ± 7 years; vitamin-D-deficient n=7 and non-deficient n=16.
sources.design: Acute prolonged exercise study stratified observationally by baseline vitamin D status; metabolomic and immune responses assessed within participants.
sources.exercise_context: 2.5 hours of cycling at 15% delta (approximately 55–60% VO2max).
sources.sampling_times: Pre-exercise, immediately post-exercise, and 1 hour post-exercise for the reported metabolite/immune response measures.
sources.biomarkers: Plasma untargeted metabolomics; leukocyte counts; bacteria-stimulated neutrophil elastase release per neutrophil after ex-vivo stimulation with extracts of Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Enterobacter aerogenes; PMA-stimulated oxidative burst.
sources.key_finding: Low vitamin D status was associated with a larger post-exercise fall in bacteria-stimulated neutrophil degranulation (elastase) at 1 hour (-43% in deficient vs approximately no change in non-deficient participants) and with different metabolomic profiles, including purine/pyrimidine catabolites and linoleic-acid-related features.
sources.clinical_endpoint: Direct ex-vivo innate immune functional co-measurement: bacteria-stimulated neutrophil degranulation (elastase release per neutrophil); PMA-stimulated oxidative burst also measured. This is not a live-pathogen killing assay and there was no prospective infection endpoint.
sources.validation: Neutrophil function was measured alongside metabolomics in the same small cohort; the group-by-time neutrophil degranulation result is a functional co-measurement, not independent validation of a specific metabolite signature. No intervention/causal mediation, external replication or infection prediction.
sources.limitations: Small all-male sample; vitamin D status was not randomized and metabolites were not shown to mediate the functional response. Bacterial-extract-stimulated elastase release is an ex-vivo degranulation assay, not pathogen killing or clinical protection; no vitamin D intervention or prospective infection follow-up. Two-and-a-half-hour cycling is a specific prolonged endurance challenge.
sources.evidence_anchor: Abstract; Methods, neutrophil degranulation / oxidative burst assays and metabolomics; Results, neutrophil responses and plasma metabolomics.
sources.integrity_notes: DOI, publication date and abstract verified in PubMed; open full text and university repository also inspected. No correction/retraction conclusion claimed.

sources.title: The exercise metabolome: acute aerobic and anaerobic signatures
sources.authors: Joseph K. Pellegrino, Tracy G. Anthony, Peter Gillies, Shawn M. Arent
sources.population: 40 healthy, physically active men and women.
sources.design: Within-participant acute comparison on separate days using discovery metabolomics.
sources.exercise_context: 45 minutes of aerobic cycling and, on a separate day, resistance exercise.
sources.sampling_times: Rest, immediately after exercise, and 1 hour post-exercise.
sources.biomarkers: Serum untargeted metabolomics, including purine turnover, substrate catabolism/mobilization, fatty-acid use and features annotated to inflammatory signaling.
sources.key_finding: Both exercise modes changed the serum metabolome immediately after exercise, with broad movement toward baseline by 1 hour. Shared changes included purine metabolism, substrate mobilization and inflammatory-signaling annotations; aerobic exercise had greater lipid/substrate diversity and resistance exercise more purine turnover/glycolytic flux.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No immune-cell functional test, infection outcome, or clinical prediction.
sources.validation: Acute modality comparison only; no independent validation or immune functional confirmation.
sources.limitations: Useful metabolic time-course reference but immune relevance is pathway annotation, not measured immune dysfunction or pathogen defense. Follow-up ends at 1 hour.
sources.evidence_anchor: Abstract; Methods, exercise and blood sampling; Results, exercise-metabolome comparison.
sources.integrity_notes: DOI and PMID verified through PubMed and full text.

sources.title: Regular moderate physical activity potentially accelerates and strengthens both the pro-inflammatory and pro-resolving lipid mediator response after acute exercise stress
sources.authors: Linda Malan, Lizelle Zandberg, Cindy Pienaar, Arista Nienaber, Lize Havemann-Nel
sources.population: 33 healthy men aged 18–35: 18 recreational runners and 15 less-active controls.
sources.design: Pre-post acute resistance challenge comparing habitual-activity groups.
sources.exercise_context: Unaccustomed multi-joint resistance exercise: three sets of 8–10 repetitions at 80% 1RM for squat, leg press and knee extension.
sources.sampling_times: Pre-exercise, immediately post, 1 hour, 2 hours, 24 hours and 72 hours.
sources.biomarkers: Plasma PUFA-derived lipid mediators 5-HETE, 15-HETE, 18-HEPE and 17-HDHA, plus leukocyte PTGES2 and ALOX15 expression.
sources.key_finding: Lipid-mediator and leukocyte gene-expression trajectories differed by habitual activity. 5- and 15-HETE changed over time in runners; 18-HEPE changed in both groups, and 17-HDHA evidence was borderline. The pattern suggests earlier or stronger mediator kinetics in runners but does not establish net immune suppression or resolution function.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No infection or immune-cell functional endpoint.
sources.validation: Within-study assay of genes and circulating lipids; no external cohort or predictive validation.
sources.limitations: Small all-male sample; runner/control grouping is non-randomized; eicosanoid-related concentrations and gene expression are proxies, not functional assays. Several tested lipid mediators did not show clear group-specific effects.
sources.evidence_anchor: Abstract; Methods, exercise protocol and blood collection; Results, mediator and gene-expression trajectories.
sources.integrity_notes: Journal DOI and the institutional repository abstract/full-text record verified. The PDF endpoint was inconsistently accessible through the search tool; bibliographic and study details were available in repository and publisher-indexed records.

sources.title: Acute exercise boosts NAD+ metabolism of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells
sources.population: Trial 1: 24 healthy young recreational runners (12 female). Trial 2: 12 healthy young adults (6 female), with lower fitness than trial 1.
sources.design: Two complementary human acute-exercise studies: randomized crossover modality comparison and a separate high-temporal-resolution exercise trial.
sources.sample_size: 36 across two separate trials (24 + 12); analysis sample counts vary by assay.
sources.exercise_context: Trial 1: time- and energy-matched treadmill HIIT versus moderate continuous running. Trial 2: 40-minute cycling at 60% VO2peak.
sources.sampling_times: Trial 1: baseline, immediately post and 1 hour post. Trial 2: baseline, after warm-up, exercise minutes 5, 10, 15 and 30, exercise cessation, and 1 hour post (eight timepoints).
sources.biomarkers: PBMC NAD+ pathway enzyme gene expression/protein and intracellular NAD+ metabolites; serum nicotinamide and related NAD+ metabolites.
sources.key_finding: Acute exercise increased PBMC NAMPT expression and intracellular NAD+; serum nicotinamide decreased. Trial 2 localized the strongest NAMPT-expression response to exercise itself, with detailed sampling showing pathway-specific timing. This is direct human immunometabolic measurement, but not an assay of antimicrobial function.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No ex-vivo immune effector assay, pathogen challenge, infection incidence or prediction model.
sources.validation: Direction of response was observed in two independent exercise trials within the same paper; no external research-group replication or infection outcome validation.
sources.limitations: Small cohorts, young adults, brief follow-up ending at 1 hour; metabolite/enzyme changes are mechanistic candidates and cannot be equated with improved or impaired host defense.
sources.evidence_anchor: Abstract; Results, PBMC NAD+ response in trials 1 and 2; Methods, acute exercise and blood/PBMC collection.
sources.integrity_notes: PubMed abstract and open author-institution full text were checked; DOI, Epub date and trial details agree.

sources.title: Temporal dynamics of the multi-omic response to endurance exercise training
sources.authors: MoTrPAC Study Group and Lead Analysts
sources.population: Male and female Fischer 344 rats; animal model only, not a human training study.
sources.design: MoTrPAC progressive treadmill endurance-training experiment with multi-tissue, multi-omic analyses.
sources.exercise_context: Eight-week progressive endurance training; tissue collection at training weeks 1, 2, 4 and 8; sedentary, sex-matched controls.
sources.sampling_times: Training timepoints 1, 2, 4 and 8 weeks; trained animals were sampled 48 hours after their last exercise bout.
sources.biomarkers: Metabolomics/lipidomics plus transcriptomics, proteomics, immunoassays, epigenomics and other platforms across whole blood, plasma and 18 solid tissues; 9,466 assays, 25 platforms, 19 tissues.
sources.key_finding: Training produced widespread tissue- and time-specific metabolic and immune-pathway changes, including inflammatory, tissue-remodeling and metabolic adaptations. This is a valuable hypothesis-generating resource for candidate pathways and time-course design.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No human clinical infection endpoint; immune pathway/analyte signals are measured in rats.
sources.validation: Public multi-omic data repository and some cross-species comparisons with published human exercise datasets; no validation as a human post-exercise infection biomarker.
sources.limitations: Animal training physiology, species and tissue differences prevent direct inference about the human open window. Training adaptation collected 48 hours after the final bout is distinct from a human acute post-bout time course.
sources.evidence_anchor: Abstract; Results, animal study design and training-regulated features; Methods and data availability.
sources.integrity_notes: Nature full text and DOI verified. Explicitly classified as animal evidence.

sources.title: Metabolomics Signatures of a Respiratory Tract Infection During an Altitude Training Camp in Elite Rowers
sources.authors: Félix Boudry, Fabienne Durand, Corentine Goossens
sources.population: 27 elite rowers (15 male, 12 female) in an altitude camp; nine developed respiratory illness (eight COVID-19 and one bronchitis).
sources.design: Observational real-world training-camp illness comparison using repeated urine metabolomics and separate comparisons intended to distinguish illness from altitude/training effects.
sources.sample_size: 27 total; illness comparison DS1 used 9 ill and 9 healthy-control samples/participants.
sources.exercise_context: 12-day altitude training camp at 1,850 m; not a standardized acute exercise challenge.
sources.sampling_times: Daily urine samples; illness-day versus each athlete's day-1 baseline, plus asymptomatic day-1/day-3 and day-1/day-8 comparisons for altitude/training context.
sources.biomarkers: Urinary 1H-NMR metabolomics; illness-associated kynurenine, N-methylnicotinamide, pyroglutamate, propionate, N-formyltryptophan, tryptophan and glucose among highlighted features.
sources.key_finding: A small illness-day versus baseline model identified a candidate urinary metabolite profile distinct from early/prolonged altitude-training comparisons. For the illness comparison, cross-validated Q2 was 0.36; the study itself calls for larger confirmation.
sources.clinical_endpoint: Clinically reported respiratory illness during the camp; infection association is present, but the metabolites were not shown to predict illness prospectively before onset or to reflect a standardized post-bout window.
sources.validation: Internal cross-validation and permutation testing only; no independent external cohort or prospective pre-symptom validation.
sources.limitations: Only nine illness cases; illness-day samples may be after symptoms began; altitude, training load and infection timing are hard to separate; urine signatures do not establish immune-cell function or exercise-caused susceptibility.
sources.evidence_anchor: Abstract; Results, baseline characteristics and illness-vs-altitude/training datasets; Methods, daily urine collection and NMR.
sources.integrity_notes: Open full text, PubMed record and DOI checked. No external validation reported in the paper.

sources.title: Identification of biomarkers of illness incidence in national team cross-country skiers using metabolomics (BJSM abstract FO15)
sources.authors: Helen Hanstock, Öyvind Karlsson, Andrew Govus, Kerry McGawley
sources.population: 23 national-team cross-country skiers, 13 male and 10 female, age 21 ± 1; illness-susceptible n=14 and non-susceptible n=8 in the reported analyses.
sources.design: Prospective athlete cohort abstract with baseline/post-exercise metabolomics and 15-week illness diary follow-up using OSTRC-H.
sources.sample_size: 23 enrolled; abstract reports 14 susceptible plus 8 non-susceptible in the analysis (one participant not represented in those group totals).
sources.exercise_context: Rest and post-maximal incremental exercise test; illness monitored during a 15-week training period.
sources.sampling_times: Rest and post-exercise; exact post-exercise interval not stated in the abstract.
sources.biomarkers: Capillary whole-blood targeted and untargeted liquid- and gas-chromatography metabolomics; 346 identified metabolites; resting glucose-6-phosphate, squalene and deoxycholic acid contributed to separation after feature selection.
sources.key_finding: A resting metabolite classifier was significant only after restricting features to VIP>1; no significant OPLS-DA model was achieved for metabolite responses to exercise. Pathway enrichment showed no significant activity differences.
sources.clinical_endpoint: Prospectively recorded illness incidence, but not a peer-reviewed full-paper analysis in this record.
sources.validation: No independent validation; exercise-response model not significant; internal feature selection risks optimism.
sources.limitations: Conference abstract only and therefore excluded by the current protocol unless a peer-reviewed full paper is located; small cohort, abstract-level methods, and no post-exercise prediction signal.
sources.evidence_anchor: Conference abstract, design, results and conclusion.
sources.integrity_notes: BJSM abstract page verified. Search did not identify a peer-reviewed full paper under this exact title; this does not prove one is absent.

sources.title: Blood Biochemical Responses to Acute Exercise: Findings from the Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium (MoTrPAC)
sources.authors: Jeremy M. Robbins et al.; MoTrPAC Study Group
sources.population: Sedentary adults in the pre-COVID MoTrPAC cohort. 176 completed the baseline acute test (EE n=66, RE n=73, CON n=37); 175 had at least one biospecimen and comprise the reported baseline analytic cohort (EE n=65, RE n=73, CON n=37). Mean age 41±15 years; 72% female. The post-training repeat cohort was much smaller.
sources.design: Randomized, multi-center endurance exercise / resistance exercise / non-exercise control acute-bout blood profiling; the paper reports cross-omic feature/time/mode analyses and baseline CCA of plasma metabolites with exercise/clinical traits. This is a bioRxiv preprint, current PMC record Version 2, and is listed separately as frontier evidence rather than peer-reviewed core evidence.
sources.sample_size: 176 completed baseline acute test (EE 66, RE 73, CON 37); 175 with ≥1 biospecimen / baseline analytic cohort (EE 65, RE 73, CON 37). Omics subsets: plasma metabolomics n=175 participants; whole-blood transcriptomics n=173; Olink plasma proteomics n=44 participants. Olink generated 378 repeated samples across 9 plates; 4 samples from 3 participants were excluded, so 374 samples remained for analysis. After QC/annotation: 1,141 plasma metabolites, 20,524 whole-blood transcripts and 1,417 plasma proteins. 45 completed a post-intervention acute retest and 44 had biospecimen collections; these follow-up omics data were not analyzed in this preprint due to low N/confounding.
sources.exercise_context: Baseline 40-minute cycling at approximately 65% VO2peak or multi-exercise resistance work to volitional fatigue; non-exercise supine control.
sources.sampling_times: Baseline and acute session sampling up to 7 timepoints over 24 h; pre-exercise; EE and CON also at 20 and 40 min; recovery at about 10 min, 30 min, 3.5 h and 24 h, with the schedule depending on randomized group/time profile. Not every participant contributes to every timepoint/omics assay.
sources.biomarkers: Plasma LC-MS metabolomics (1,141 metabolites across 4 targeted and 6 untargeted platforms; n=175 participants), PAXgene whole-blood transcriptomics (20,524 transcripts; n=173), and Olink plasma proteomics (1,417 proteins; n=44 participants / 378 repeated samples before exclusion of 4 sample outliers from 3 participants). 7,066 transcripts, 189 proteins and 448 metabolites were differentially abundant vs non-exercise control. Cross-omic and time/mode comparisons were performed, but assay coverage was unbalanced; baseline metabolome was also integrated with clinical/exercise phenotypes by CCA.
sources.key_finding: The study reports temporal and modality-dependent blood responses across transcriptomic, plasma protein and metabolite data; many analytes changed over time in controls too. RNA-based immune-cell/pathway signatures (including early NK/CD8, neutrophil and broader immune-effector annotations) and lipid-metabolic features are hypothesis-generating; the study did not measure immune-cell effector function or pathogen defense. Cross-omic breadth does not make every signal a jointly validated immune biomarker.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No infection incidence, pathogen challenge, vaccine response or direct immune effector-function outcome. Whole-blood transcriptomic signals cannot fully distinguish cell-composition shifts from per-cell activation; targeted Olink coverage constrained enrichment analysis.
sources.validation: Randomized exercise/control contrast, repeated sampling and multi-omic analysis within one cohort; no independent cohort validation and no infection-risk prediction. The small post-training data (45 retests / 44 biospecimen collections) were not analyzed.
sources.limitations: Preprint, not peer reviewed as of 2026-10-02. Assay subsets differ sharply (metabolomics 175, transcriptomics 173, Olink proteomics 44 participants), and repeated Olink sample count is not participant count; several timepoint/group cells are small. Whole-blood RNA is sensitive to cell mobilization and cannot unambiguously identify per-cell activation; no direct PBMC/neutrophil function or clinical infection endpoint. Baseline analytic cohort was sedentary, pre-COVID and not representative of trained athletes; acute exercise prescription is specific.
sources.evidence_anchor: Current PMC/bioRxiv Version 2; Abstract; Results, research design/clinical characteristics and analyte/time-course findings; STAR Methods, omics sample sizes, sampling and Olink QC.
sources.integrity_notes: The public bioRxiv version API records Version 1 posted 2026-03-04 and Version 2 posted 2026-03-11; current PMC full text is explicitly labeled [Version 2]. DOI 10.64898/2026.03.02.704798 is the versioned record identifier without a v2 suffix. This is a preprint and had not been peer reviewed as of the cutoff; keep in a separate frontier/preprint table, not the peer-reviewed core.

sources.title: Multiomics profiling identifies molecular and cellular signatures of regular exercise in human peripheral blood
sources.population: 86 non-obese adults ages 20–40 in the Chinese Immune Multi-Omics Atlas reanalysis: 40 self-reported regular exercisers and 46 sedentary controls.
sources.design: Cross-sectional comparison of habitual activity groups using existing cohort blood data; no exercise intervention or acute post-bout sampling.
sources.exercise_context: Regular exercise exposure defined by self-reported habitual activity; fasting morning plasma and immune-cell profiles compared between groups.
sources.sampling_times: Single fasting morning blood collection; no exercise-linked time course reported.
sources.biomarkers: Plasma metabolomics and lipidomics integrated with single-cell PBMC transcriptomics and chromatin-accessibility profiles.
sources.key_finding: Regular exercise was associated with plasma signatures consistent with fatty-acid oxidation and antioxidant metabolism, alongside APC antigen-presentation transcription/accessibility and epigenetic priming of CD8 cytotoxic T and mature NK-cell effector programs. Cell-cell communication analyses inferred greater MHC-I/II signaling and lower inflammatory networks.
sources.clinical_endpoint: No acute immune function assay, pathogen challenge, or prospective infection outcome; intercellular communication and effector readiness are molecular/inferred features.
sources.validation: Multi-layer concordance within existing cohort data; no longitudinal training intervention or external infection-risk validation.
sources.limitations: Cross-sectional exposure, small selected sample and self-reported activity; causality/direction cannot be established. This informs training-associated immune phenotype but does not map the acute open-window trajectory.
sources.evidence_anchor: PubMed abstract; publication date and DOI; sample details verified against the study authors' institutional report.
sources.integrity_notes: Peer-reviewed journal metadata and abstract verified in PubMed; exact group counts and CIMA reanalysis details checked against the authors' institutional report.

findings.claim: The most direct metabolomics-to-immune-function human evidence in this set is the small Jones et al. study: prolonged cycling, vitamin D stratification, plasma metabolomics and bacteria-stimulated neutrophil degranulation were measured together. It gives a plausible signal of effect modification, but does not show that the metabolite pattern causes dysfunction or predicts infection.
findings.certainty: moderate for the measured within-study association; low for causal or predictive interpretation
findings.protocol_implication: Separate metabolite abundance/pathway association from a directly measured immune function assay; extract the function assay's stimulus, cell type, and post-bout timepoint.

findings.claim: Acute human exercise metabolomics is dynamic and often dominated by generic energetic, purine, lipid-substrate and stress responses. Contrepois and Pellegrino show immediate-to-1-hour trajectories, while the MoTrPAC human preprint maps additional time- and mode-dependent analytes out to 24 hours; this does not by itself establish an open-window deficit.
findings.certainty: high for temporal blood-metabolome perturbation; low for immune functional meaning
findings.protocol_implication: Chart raw metabolite classes, tissue source and time since exercise separately from immune pathway annotation or measured immune function.

findings.claim: Lipid mediators and NAD+ pathway metabolites are promising immune-adjacent candidates with actual human blood/PBMC measurements. Current studies are small, stop by 72 hours (lipid mediators) or 1 hour (NAD+), and lack infection or pathogen-defense validation.
findings.certainty: moderate for observed molecular responses; low for implications to infection susceptibility
findings.protocol_implication: Use separate candidate classes for systemic lipid mediators and cell-intrinsic PBMC metabolites; record whether any downstream response was directly assayed.

findings.claim: There are emerging infection-linked metabolomics observations, but they do not yet establish validated post-exercise prediction: the 2025 rower study detects illness-day urine differences in nine cases; the 2024 skier conference abstract reports a resting model but no significant exercise-response model and is ineligible under the current source-type rule.
findings.protocol_implication: Extract infection timing/definition, whether samples precede symptoms, prospective follow-up, model validation and sensitivity/specificity. Keep conference abstracts out of the included-source evidence set unless a full paper is found.

findings.claim: MoTrPAC materially expands multi-omic discovery resources, but the evidence type matters: its 2024 training atlas is rat-only; the 2026 acute human blood analysis is a preprint and still lacks direct immune function or infection outcomes; the 2026 regular-exercise immune atlas is cross-sectional rather than an acute challenge.
findings.certainty: high for the stated study designs and omic breadth; low for application to acute infection vulnerability
findings.protocol_implication: Maintain explicit design/species/publication-status strata and do not combine these sources as equivalent human acute-window evidence.

gaps: Few studies co-measure untargeted/targeted metabolomics with cell-specific immune functional assays after acute exercise; most multi-omics integrates molecular layers but not a functional infection-defense outcome.

Prospective infection incidence is rarely paired with acute pre/post-exercise metabolite sampling. The 2024 skier report located here is conference-abstract-only and its post-exercise model was non-significant; the 2025 rower illness samples may follow symptom onset.
Follow-up to 24–72 hours is uncommon in large human metabolomics datasets, while immediate changes can be transient and resolution kinetics can differ by modality, fitness and participant status.
Analytical platforms, metabolite identification confidence, pathway annotations, food/fasting control, plasma-volume shifts and exercise-dose reporting vary substantially.
The newest habitual-exercise immune multi-omics evidence is cross-sectional and cannot separate training adaptation from selection, diet, body composition or reverse causality.
proposed_updates: Keep acute-bout challenge and longitudinal training as separate evidence strata; add a separate stratum for habitual-activity cross-sectional studies and label all animal studies distinctly.

Reframe the 30-minute rule: include a study when it has at least one post-bout observation at or beyond 30 minutes, but preserve immediate/0–10-minute samples as early kinetics. Studies ending before 30 minutes can be excluded or listed as boundary evidence; do not discard an otherwise eligible study merely because it also samples immediately.

Require every multi-omics record to state which assay was applied to which matrix/cell type and whether layers were statistically integrated, merely measured in parallel, or tied to an immune functional outcome.

Use a tiered evidence map: molecular abundance or enrichment; direct immune-cell function; prospective infection association; externally validated prediction. Never promote pathway enrichment, inferred signaling, or cell counts to functional suppression or infection prediction.

Prespecify charting of exercise modality, dose/intensity and relative intensity, training status, sex, nutritional/fasting controls, collection matrix, exact sampling times, metabolite assay/annotation confidence, cell composition, plasma-volume correction, and immune assay stimulus/readout.

For infection studies, chart the infection case definition, ascertainment method, onset relative to exercise and sample collection, event follow-up duration, model development/validation split, calibration/discrimination and external replication.
search_limitations: This is a targeted public-web evidence scan, not formal database searching or the registered scoping review. PubMed/PMC and publisher records were surfaced via web search; no subscription database export, duplicate removal, screening log or exhaustive citation chaining was performed.

Some PMC pages and ScienceDirect/repository endpoints intermittently returned CAPTCHA, 403, 401 or timeout responses; PubMed abstracts, publisher search-indexed text, institutional repositories and publicly indexed full-text records were used to verify the included details.

The MoTrPAC acute human blood paper was identified as a bioRxiv preprint as of the cutoff and must remain labeled preprint unless a peer-reviewed version available by 2026-10-02 is confirmed in the formal restart.
A limited title-specific retraction/correction search was run for selected key records and returned no notice; this does not constitute an exhaustive integrity check across all records or databases.

The BJSM skier metabolomics report is a conference abstract. It is shown as an excluded boundary record because the supplied protocol excludes abstracts without peer-reviewed full-text versions; a formal search should check for a subsequent full paper.
